title: The Potrero and the Hand: Fiorito, Naples, and the Sixty Years of a National Saint
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Lanús, birth at the Policlínico Evita
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The fifth child of Diego Chitoro Maradona and Dalma Salvadora Franco is born in the public polyclinic at Lanús, a hospital that carries Eva Perón's name, on the last Sunday of October. The family lives in Villa Fiorito, an unpaved shantytown south of the capital where the streets end at a drainage ditch and the houses are brick and sheet metal. Argentina has been five years without Perón and will wait thirteen more to have him back. The boy is registered as Diego Armando. Nobody writes down the hour.
suggested_refs: The Policlínico Evita, later Hospital Presidente Perón, Lanús

stops.name: Villa Fiorito, the first ball
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the pool gives the year 1963 only, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: At about three years old he is given a football and, by every account of his childhood, does not let go of it again. He learns the game on the potrero, the vacant lot of dirt and stones where the barrio's boys play until the light fails, a few streets from the open ditch. Villa Fiorito has no paving and no plumbing; it has a thousand of these lots. He will name the place for the rest of his life as the source of everything he became, and never once as something he escaped.
suggested_refs: The potreros of Villa Fiorito, Lomas de Zamora
sources: Vice, 'The Nativity: Where Diego Maradona Comes From'

stops.name: La Paternal, Los Cebollitas
stops.date_confidence: month attested for joining Los Cebollitas; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: A scout watches the eight-year-old play for a club called Estrella Roja and takes him across the city to Argentinos Juniors, where he joins Los Cebollitas, the Little Onions. The junior team wins two Evita Tournaments and, by the count the country has repeated ever since, goes a hundred and forty-one matches without losing. At halftime in the first division the boy is sent out alone to juggle a ball in front of the crowd, and the crowd stays in its seats to watch a child keep a ball off the ground.
suggested_refs: Team photographs of Los Cebollitas, Argentinos Juniors youth side, 1969-1975

stops.name: La Paternal, the debut at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He comes on for Argentinos Juniors in the first division ten days before his sixteenth birthday, wearing number 16. The ground is the one that will carry his name from 2004, when the club renames it for its centenary. He has been performing here for years already, at halftime, as the boy who keeps the ball off the ground; now the match is running and he is on the field against grown men with families, the smallest person on the pitch, and the crowd that came for them stays for him.
suggested_refs: Argentinos Juniors first-team sheet, 20 October 1976

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the first goals
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Three and a half weeks after the debut, Argentinos travel to the coast to play San Lorenzo de Mar del Plata at the Estadio General San Martín. He scores twice, two minutes apart, both past the goalkeeper Rubén Lucangioli, in a five to two win. The record will be copied wrongly for decades, into Buenos Aires and onto the other San Lorenzo, the one from Almagro. The goals themselves are not in dispute; only the place moves, four hundred kilometres back toward the capital.
suggested_refs: Match report, Argentinos Juniors 5-2 San Lorenzo de Mar del Plata, 14 November 1976
sources: La Capital de Mar del Plata, 'A 48 años de los primeros goles de Maradona'
El Gráfico, 'A 40 años de los primeros goles'

stops.name: La Bombonera, capped at sixteen and left off the list
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the pool gives the place only as Buenos Aires, and La Bombonera as the ground is a reconstruction
stops.campa: Four months after his sixteenth birthday he plays his first match for Argentina, against Hungary. A year later César Luis Menotti leaves him off the squad for the World Cup that Argentina will host and win, judging seventeen too young; the junta's tournament goes on without him and he watches it from outside. In June 1979 he scores his first senior international goal, at Hampden Park in Glasgow. The team that won without him will not win again until it is his.
suggested_refs: The 1978 Argentina squad list, from which he is absent

stops.name: Tokyo, the youth world title
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's geography entry dated this final 1 June 1979, which is wrong by three months
stops.campa: At the National Stadium in Tokyo he captains Argentina to the World Youth Championship, beating the Soviet Union three to one in the final before fifty-two thousand people, with six goals across the tournament and the award for its best player. It is the first time the world outside Argentina watches him for a whole competition. He is eighteen. Between this and the senior trophy stand seven years, one broken ankle, two world record transfers, and a city in southern Italy that does not yet know his name.
suggested_refs: Film of the 1979 FIFA World Youth Championship final, National Stadium, Tokyo
sources: Wikipedia, '1979 FIFA World Youth Championship final'

segments.name: Boca, Barcelona, and the Record Fees

stops.name: La Bombonera, signed for Boca
stops.date_confidence: attested; he signed on 20 February and debuted two days later, not four as the pool had it
stops.campa: He signs for Boca Juniors, the club he supported as a boy in Fiorito, on the twentieth of February, and two days later he is on the field against Talleres de Córdoba, scoring twice in a four to one win. Boca take the Metropolitano that year. La Bombonera is a stand of concrete that shakes when the crowd jumps, and for the rest of his life, through Barcelona and Naples and Seville, he will describe himself as a man on loan from this ground. He is twenty years old.
stops.quote: Le agradezco a Dios que haya creado La Bombonera y que me haya hecho de Boca.
stops.quote_source: Farewell speech at La Bombonera, 10 November 2001, transcript reproduced in Los Andes
suggested_refs: Boca Juniors 4-1 Talleres de Córdoba, 22 February 1981, match record

stops.name: Sarrià, sent off against Brazil
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Argentina come to the 1982 World Cup as holders and he plays every minute of all five matches. Italy's Claudio Gentile marks him out of the second-round game with a hand on his shirt for ninety minutes. Against Brazil at Sarrià, three goals down and minutes from elimination, he kicks João Batista in the thigh and is sent off in front of forty-four thousand people. It is the first World Cup he leaves early, and it is not the last; the holders go out in the second round and he is twenty-one.
suggested_refs: Estadi de Sarrià, demolished 1997; Brazil 3-1 Argentina, 2 July 1982

stops.name: Barcelona, the world record fee
stops.date_confidence: month attested; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Barcelona pay about five million pounds for him, a world record, and he arrives in a city that has taken in foreign masters before: Cristóbal Balenciaga opened his Barcelona house here in 1935 and dressed Europe out of it. The Catalan club expects a season of miracles from a twenty-one-year-old and gets hepatitis instead, then a broken ankle, then a brawl in front of the king. Two years later they sell him for more than they paid, to the poorest big club in Italy.
suggested_refs: The 1982 Barcelona transfer papers, then the largest fee in the game

stops.name: Camp Nou, the ankle broken by Goikoetxea
stops.date_confidence: month attested; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He loses part of his first season to hepatitis. In September of the second, Athletic Bilbao's Andoni Goikoetxea comes through the back of his left ankle and breaks it, and he is out for months again, the second long absence in two years at a club that paid a world record for his presence. He is twenty-two, and of his two seasons in Catalonia he spends the better part of one waiting to be fit. The football Naples will see is played on this ankle, and the pain that comes with it will be managed by whatever is at hand to manage it.
suggested_refs: Television footage of Goikoetxea's tackle, September 1983
sources: El Mundo Deportivo and La Vanguardia, September 1983

stops.name: Madrid, the brawl at the Bernabéu
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool dated this event twice and wrongly, as June 1984 in Madrid and as 5 September 1984 at the Camp Nou
stops.campa: The Copa del Rey final is played at the Santiago Bernabéu with King Juan Carlos in the stand, and Athletic Bilbao win it one to nothing. After the whistle the two teams fight on the pitch in front of the king and the cameras: he headbutts one opponent and elbows another, and three players a side are suspended for months. It is the last thing he does in a Barcelona shirt. The club that bought the best player in the world sells him two months later.
suggested_refs: Televised footage of the 1984 Copa del Rey final melee, Santiago Bernabéu

segments.name: Naples, the Poor South Buys a God

stops.name: Naples, the city that has been waiting
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival; the cocaine use is dated 1985 in the pool and that year is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He arrives in a city that has never won the Italian championship, in the country's poor south, jeered as a matter of routine in the northern stadiums. Napoli have paid a new world record to get him. This is the Naples where Pasquale Simonetti was shot dead in 1955 and his pregnant widow Pupetta Maresca killed the man she held responsible, and the cocaine trade runs through the same streets; within a year he is using it regularly and the club is fining him for the training he misses.
suggested_refs: The Naples of the mid-1980s: the port, the Quartieri Spagnoli, the Giuliano clan trials

stops.name: Stadio San Paolo, presented to seventy-five thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Seventy-five thousand people fill the San Paolo to watch him warm up. He has not played a match for Napoli, has not kicked a ball for them, and the stadium is full at the price of a ticket to see him stand on the grass in a light blue shirt. The fee that brought him is about six point nine million pounds, a world record for the second time in two years. The city has bought one impossible thing the way a poor family buys one impossible thing, and for the next seven years everything Naples wants to say about itself it says through him.
suggested_refs: Press photographs of the presentation at the Stadio San Paolo, 5 July 1984

stops.name: Puebla, the draw with Italy
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool dated this match 2 June and called it a win, both wrong
stops.campa: Argentina meet the holders at the Estadio Cuauhtémoc in Puebla in the group stage. Alessandro Altobelli scores from a penalty in the sixth minute; Maradona equalises in the thirty-fourth and the match ends level. He is twenty-five and he is captain, and the team around him is ordinary enough that the tournament will afterward be told as one man's. Four years earlier Italy put Gentile on him and knocked Argentina out. This time they take a point off him and go out in the next round.
suggested_refs: Italy 1-1 Argentina, Estadio Cuauhtémoc, 5 June 1986
sources: Wikipedia, '1986 FIFA World Cup Group A'

stops.name: Estadio Azteca, the hand and the run
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the quarter-final against England, four years after the Falklands war, he punches the ball over Peter Shilton in the fifty-first minute and the referee gives the goal. Four minutes later he takes the ball inside his own half, beats five England players across sixty metres of grass and scores again. The two goals are four minutes apart and are the two halves of him: the theft nobody caught, and the thing nobody else could do. A FIFA poll in 2002 votes the second the greatest goal ever scored at a World Cup.
stops.quote: Un poco con la cabeza de Maradona y otro poco con la mano de Dios.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to a post-match remark, Mexico City, 22 June 1986; widely reported in at least two wordings, not confirmed against a primary transcript
suggested_refs: Film of both goals, Argentina 2-1 England, Estadio Azteca, 22 June 1986
sources: FIFA World Cup 1986 official match record

stops.name: Estadio Azteca, the trophy
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Argentina beat West Germany three to two in the final at the Azteca, twice ahead, twice pegged back, and winning it late. He goes up the steps as captain and lifts the cup over a stadium of more than a hundred thousand people. The Golden Ball for the tournament's best player is voted to him unanimously. He is twenty-five years old, and everything he does across the remaining thirty-four years of his life will be measured against this afternoon. Argentina will wait thirty-six years for the next one.
suggested_refs: The 1986 World Cup trophy presentation, Estadio Azteca
sources: FIFA World Cup 1986 final match record

stops.name: Naples, the son he does not name
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Cristiana Sinagra gives birth in Naples to a son, Diego, twelve weeks after the World Cup final. He denies that the child is his and goes on denying it; an Italian court rules against him in 1993 when he refuses to take a DNA test. Diego Junior grows up in the same city, watching his father play for it, unacknowledged for thirty years. The reconciliation comes in 2016, four years before his father's death, and in 2021 Argentine justice confirms him among five recognised heirs.
suggested_refs: The 1993 Italian paternity ruling in Sinagra v Maradona

stops.name: Stadio San Paolo, the first scudetto
stops.date_confidence: May 1987 attested; the day is the pool's and is not corroborated elsewhere here
stops.campa: Napoli win the Italian championship for the first time in the club's history, and take the Coppa Italia in the same season, four to nothing on aggregate over Atalanta. On a wall by the city cemetery Naples writes a line to its dead, who did not live to see it. In Milan, Silvio Berlusconi has just bought the club that will become the north's answer to this, and what follows between them is played out as a war between two Italies with a ball in the middle of it.
suggested_refs: The 1986-87 Serie A table; the cemetery wall inscription in Naples

stops.name: Stadio San Paolo, the UEFA Cup
stops.date_confidence: May 1989 attested; the two-legged final against Stuttgart was completed away from Naples, and this pin marks the home leg
stops.campa: Napoli win the UEFA Cup over two legs against Stuttgart, five to four on aggregate, the only European trophy in the club's history. He is captain. The team is his and the city knows exactly what it has: a championship, a European cup, and a second championship coming the following spring. He is twenty-eight. In under two years he will be banned for fifteen months, wanted by Italian prosecutors, and gone from Naples for good. Napoli have not won a European trophy since.
suggested_refs: The 1989 UEFA Cup final, Napoli against VfB Stuttgart

stops.name: Stadio San Paolo, the night he asks Naples to choose
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Napoli have taken a second championship in May. In July the World Cup semi-final brings Italy to his own stadium, and he asks the Neapolitans out loud to support Argentina, on the grounds that Italy remembers the south only when it needs the south. Some of them do. Argentina win on penalties and put the hosts out of their own tournament, and from that night the peninsula treats him as an enemy. The Argentine anthem is whistled wherever he plays, and the Italian press does not forgive him for having asked.
suggested_refs: Italy 1-1 Argentina, penalties 3-4, Stadio San Paolo, 3 July 1990

stops.name: Stadio Olimpico, the final lost
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The final in Rome is played against West Germany in a stadium that whistles the Argentine anthem from the first note. Germany win it one to nothing with a penalty five minutes from time that Argentina dispute to this day. He weeps on the pitch and is booed while he does it, and booed again on the podium. He has been in two finals and won one, and this is the last World Cup match he plays as a man to whom the tournament belongs. He is twenty-nine years old.
suggested_refs: The 1990 World Cup final, Stadio Olimpico, Rome
sources: FIFA World Cup 1990 final match record

stops.name: Stadio San Paolo, the positive test
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A sample taken after a Napoli match comes back positive for cocaine and he is banned from football for fifteen months. The Naples years end there: the club, the city, and the warrants tied to the cocaine and prostitution trade of the same streets that fed him. He leaves Italy in disgrace and the courts follow him out. Seven years later he goes back voluntarily to testify about doping in Italian football, and tells the reporters that he trusts the magistrates.
stops.quote: Tengo total confianza en los magistrados italianos y noto que el juez quiere investigar cuestiones que yo ya había denunciado.
stops.quote_source: To reporters on arriving in Italy to testify before judge Raffaele Guariniello, 28 November 1998; La Nación, 'Maradona declaró por su caso de doping de 1991'
suggested_refs: The FIGC disciplinary file on the March 1991 positive

stops.name: Caballito, the arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool placed this arrest in Villa Devoto, eight kilometres west of where it happened
stops.campa: Six weeks after the ban, police take him in a flat in Caballito, in Buenos Aires, with two other men, on charges of cocaine possession. The images go around the world within a day: the best player alive, five years after Mexico, walked out of a doorway by the drug squad in his own city. He is thirty years old. Argentina, which has spent five years calling him a god, watches the arrest on the evening news and carries on calling him one. The ban still has more than a year to run.
suggested_refs: Press photographs of the Caballito arrest, 26 April 1991
sources: Washington Post and Deseret News, 27 April 1991
Gulf News, 'April 26, 1991: Maradona held by drug squad'

stops.name: Seville, the season with Bilardo
stops.date_confidence: month attested; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Sevilla sign him when the ban expires and put him under Carlos Bilardo, the manager who built the 1986 team around him and won a World Cup by doing it. He has not played a competitive match in fifteen months. It does not work. He plays one season in Andalusia, out of condition and out of favour, and the club lets him go. Six years after Mexico the same two men produce a season nobody records and a quiet separation. He is thirty-two and out of European football for good.
suggested_refs: Sevilla FC squad photographs, 1992-93

stops.name: Rosario, the months at Newell's
stops.date_confidence: the pool gives 1993-1994; month and day inferred from the start of the season and defaulted
stops.campa: He signs for Newell's Old Boys and moves to Rosario, the city where Che Guevara was born, whose face he wears tattooed on his left arm. He plays a handful of matches, overweight and unhappy, and it is over within months. Rosario keeps him anyway: five years later three men in this city found a church in his name and put its Christmas on his birthday. He is thirty-three and out of a club, four months from a World Cup he still intends to play. It is his last club in Argentina before Boca take him back.
suggested_refs: Newell's Old Boys squad records, 1993-94

stops.name: Moreno, the air rifle
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool dated this 25 February, three weeks late
stops.campa: Journalists camp outside his weekend house in Moreno, west of the capital, and he comes out with a compressed-air rifle and fires into them, wounding four. The wounded are named in court: Talamoni, Zani, Vijande Rivera, Yohai. He receives a suspended sentence of more than two years, handed down in 1998, and the footage becomes the standard illustration of the years between the ban and the comeback. Four months later he is in the Argentina squad for the World Cup in the United States.
suggested_refs: Television footage of the Moreno shooting, 2 February 1994

stops.name: Foxborough, the goal, the camera, and the sample
stops.date_confidence: the Greece goal is 21 June 1994; the sample that failed for ephedrine was taken after the Nigeria match on 25 June, and the expulsion followed on 30 June. The pool merged the two matches
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of June he scores against Greece at Foxboro Stadium and runs to a pitchside camera and screams into the lens with his eyes wide open, a photograph that will be printed against him for the rest of his life. Four days later he plays Nigeria on the same field, Argentina win, and a nurse leads him off the pitch by the hand for the drug test. The sample comes back positive for ephedrine. It is the last World Cup match of his life and he does not know it while he is playing it.
stops.quote: Quiero que les quede claro a todos los argentinos que no corrí por la droga, corrí por la camiseta.
stops.quote_source: To Adrián Paenza, Dallas, 30 June 1994; ESPN transcript, 'Maradona en Estados Unidos 1994'
suggested_refs: The photograph of the celebration into the camera lens, 21 June 1994

stops.name: Dallas, the room at the team hotel
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool placed these words in Buenos Aires, and they were spoken in Dallas
stops.campa: FIFA expel him from the tournament on the thirtieth of June. In a room at the Argentina team hotel in Dallas, in Juan Marcos Franchi's room, he sits in front of a camera with the journalist Adrián Paenza and says the sentence Argentina will quote for thirty years, about his legs being cut off. He swears on his daughters that he took nothing in order to play. His international career ends here, at thirty-four goals in ninety-one matches, and he is thirty-three years old.
stops.quote: No quiero dramatizar, pero creeme que me cortaron las piernas. A mí, a mi familia, a los que están al lado mío. Ahora nos sacaron la ilusión. Y creo que me sacaron del fútbol definitivamente. Tengo los brazos caídos, el alma destrozada.
stops.quote_source: Televised statement to Adrián Paenza, Argentina team hotel, Dallas, 30 June 1994; ESPN Argentina transcript
suggested_refs: The Paenza interview footage, 30 June 1994
sources: Infobae, on the making of the Paenza interview

stops.name: Estadio Monumental, the last match
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool had him playing a farewell at La Bombonera on his birthday, which is the wrong ground and the wrong day
stops.campa: He comes back to Boca for two more seasons, heavier each year. On the twenty-fifth of October he plays a Superclasico at River Plate's Monumental, is taken off at half-time for a nineteen-year-old named Juan Román Riquelme, and Boca win two to one. Five days later, on his thirty-seventh birthday, he announces that he has finished. The country has been waiting years for a farewell match and does not get one. The last time he walks off a pitch as a professional, he is being substituted at half-time in a derby.
suggested_refs: River Plate 1-2 Boca Juniors, Estadio Monumental, 25 October 1997
sources: beIN Sports, 'Maradona's Last Game For Boca Juniors'

stops.name: Rosario, the church that keeps his birthday
stops.date_confidence: founding attested, 30 October 1998
stops.campa: A year after the retirement, three men in Rosario, Héctor Campomar, Alejandro Verón and Hernán Amez, found a church in his name on his thirty-eighth birthday and write it Ten Commandments. Its Christmas falls on the thirtieth of October. It will count members in Argentina, Mexico, Spain, Italy, Germany, Japan and England. He is overweight, addicted and out of work on the day they do it, and the canonisation runs twenty-two years ahead of the death, which here is not a contradiction.
suggested_refs: The Ten Commandments of the Iglesia Maradoniana

stops.name: Havana, the clinic and the friend
stops.date_confidence: the pool gives 2000-2004 for the Havana stays; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He goes to Cuba for treatment and stays, on and off, for four years at the Clínica La Pradera in Havana, through the worst of the addiction. Fidel Castro receives him, argues with him, keeps writing to him; he has Castro's face tattooed on his left leg and calls him a second father. In January 2015 Castro publishes the letters the two of them exchanged, in which Maradona writes that loyalty has no price and that ideas are not negotiated. Castro dies in November 2016, four years and nine days before he does.
stops.quote: Fidel, si algo he aprendido contigo a lo largo de años de sincera y hermosa amistad, es que la lealtad no tiene precio, que un amigo vale más que todo el oro del mundo, y que las ideas no se negocian.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Maradona to Fidel Castro, January 2015, published by Castro; Diario Jornada, 'Fidel Castro publicó cartas que intercambió con Maradona'
suggested_refs: The Castro tattoo on his left leg; the two letters published in Cuba, January 2015

stops.name: La Bombonera, the testimonial
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Boca fill La Bombonera for his testimonial four years after he stopped playing. He is forty-one and he cannot run, and the stadium does not care. At the end, with the microphone in his hand, he says the sentence that will follow him into every obituary written about him: that he made the mistakes and he paid for them, and that the ball is not stained. Argentina has been arguing about him for twenty years and stops arguing for one night. Nineteen years of his life remain.
stops.quote: El fútbol es el deporte más lindo y más sano del mundo. De eso no le quepa la menor duda a nadie. Porque se equivoque uno, no tiene que pagar el fútbol. Yo me equivoqué y pagué, pero la pelota no se mancha.
stops.quote_source: Farewell speech at La Bombonera, 10 November 2001, full transcript reproduced in Los Andes
suggested_refs: Film of the 10 November 2001 farewell speech
sources: Los Andes, full transcript of the farewell speech

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the stomach stapled
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool named a different clinic, eight kilometres inland from the one that operated
stops.campa: He arrives at a clinic in Cartagena de Indias weighing a hundred and twenty-one kilos, and a surgeon named Francisco Holguín performs a gastric bypass on him in about two hours. He credits the operation with saving his life. The body that beat five Englishmen in a straight line has spent a decade being kept alive by other people's decisions about it: clinics in Havana, a bypass in Colombia, and cardiological warnings that will be read out in a courtroom in San Isidro twenty-one years later.
suggested_refs: The Medihelp clinic, Bocagrande, Cartagena
sources: CBC Sports, 'Maradona undergoes stomach staple surgery'

stops.name: Luna Park, the last night of La Noche del 10
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool gave the programme a 2005-2007 run and staged the Pelé episode at the Monumental
stops.campa: Argentine television gives him a programme of his own for one season, thirteen weeks on Canal 13. Pelé sits with him in the studio for the first episode, the argument of forty years staged as a courtesy, and the show takes forty rating points. The finale is played at the Luna Park in front of five thousand people, in the hall where Charly Garcia has been putting Buenos Aires on its feet since the seventies. The run goes from August to the seventh of November and Canal 13 does not renew it.
suggested_refs: Recording of the La Noche del 10 debut with Pelé, 15 August 2005

stops.name: Buenos Aires, given the national team
stops.date_confidence: November 2008 attested; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Argentine federation makes him head coach of the national team, twenty-two years after he won a World Cup for it and fourteen after he was thrown out of one. He has coached almost nothing. He is hired because he is Maradona, which is the reason anybody does anything with him after 1994. The squad he inherits contains a twenty-one-year-old from Rosario named Lionel Messi, who has been called his successor since he was seventeen and will spend a decade being measured against a single afternoon in Mexico.
suggested_refs: The AFA announcement of his appointment, November 2008

stops.name: Cape Town, four goals to Germany
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool placed this match at Soccer City in Johannesburg, which is the wrong stadium and the wrong city
stops.campa: Germany take Argentina apart at Green Point Stadium in Cape Town in front of sixty-four thousand people, four to nothing, three of them in the last twenty-five minutes. He leaves the job within weeks. A fortnight before the match he had answered Pelé, who criticised him in public, by telling him to go back to the museum. At the end he stands on the touchline in a grey suit with his hands at his sides and watches the fourth go in. It is his last match in charge of Argentina.
stops.quote: Le pediría a Pelé y a Platini que miren alguna vez la pelota, que se dediquen a ver si es buena o mala y se dejen de hablar boludeces de mí.
stops.quote_source: Press remarks in South Africa, 16 June 2010, quoted in El Informador (Guadalajara), 'Maradona le responde a Pelé'
suggested_refs: Argentina 0-4 Germany, Green Point Stadium, 3 July 2010

stops.name: Culiacán, coaching Dorados
stops.date_confidence: the pool gives 2018-2019; month and day inferred from the season start and defaulted
stops.campa: After a season at Al Wasl in Dubai that ends in dismissal, he takes a second-division club in Culiacán, capital of Sinaloa, a city known outside Mexico for one export. Dorados go close to promotion twice with him on the bench and miss it twice. He conducts the matches from a plastic chair by the touchline, knees swollen, walking with a stick, and the stands fill anyway, for him and not for the second division. He is fifty-seven years old and it is his last job outside Argentina.
suggested_refs: Dorados de Sinaloa match footage, 2018-19 Ascenso MX season

stops.name: La Plata, the last job
stops.date_confidence: September 2019 attested; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Gimnasia y Esgrima La Plata, at the bottom of the Argentine first division, hire him in September, and the queue for season tickets goes around the block. He can barely walk to the bench. He stays until he dies, thirteen months later. El Bosque, the small ground at the corner of Avenida 60 and calle 118, is the last place in the world where he goes to work, and the opposing supporters stand up for him when he arrives, every week, in every stadium in the country.
suggested_refs: Estadio Juan Carmelo Zerillo, El Bosque, La Plata
sources: Club Gimnasia y Esgrima La Plata records

stops.name: La Plata, the sixtieth birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He turns sixty at the Gimnasia ground on a Friday in a pandemic, wearing a mask, helped along the touchline by two men, and leaves the match after a few minutes. The photographs from that afternoon are the ones the country will see again four weeks later on every front page. Three days after the birthday he is admitted to a clinic in La Plata. Twenty-six days after it he is dead. Fiorito to a potrero to Naples to a bench at the corner of Avenida 60 is sixty years and twenty-six days.
suggested_refs: Press photographs of the 60th birthday at El Bosque, 30 October 2020

stops.name: Olivos, the clot
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool had him admitted and discharged in La Plata, and the surgery and discharge were at Olivos
stops.campa: He is admitted in La Plata with anaemia and dehydration and moved to the Clínica Olivos in Vicente López, where a scan finds a subdural haematoma. Leopoldo Luque operates on the third of November and the clot is drained. Eight days later he is discharged, and instead of a clinic he is taken to a rented house in Tigre with a rota of nurses and no medical equipment. The decision to send him there is the centre of everything that follows, in the courts and in the country.
suggested_refs: The Clínica Olivos, Vicente López; coordinates approximate

stops.name: Benavídez, the house at lot 45
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool and English Wikipedia both carry the early-report locality Dique Lujan, nine kilometres east of the house
stops.campa: He dies in the house at lot 45 of the San Andrés gated community in Benavídez, Tigre, twenty-two days after brain surgery. The autopsy records acute pulmonary oedema over an exacerbated chronic heart failure, and an agony of some twelve hours, not the sleep the first bulletins described. Seven of the people responsible for his care are charged with homicide by eventual intent. The first trial collapses in 2025 when the judge is found to have been filming a documentary in her own courtroom.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the house at lot 45, San Andrés, Benavídez, published in the trial record

stops.name: Casa Rosada, the queue
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The government lays him in state in the Casa Rosada and declares three days of national mourning. Tens of thousands come through the palace where Eva Perón's crowds filled the square below, and where Cristina Fernández de Kirchner took the presidential oath in 2007. The queue runs for blocks, the doors are closed early, the crowd forces them. Argentina has queued for a coffin like this once before, in 1952, and everybody standing in the line knows which one.
suggested_refs: Aerial photographs of the queue at the Casa Rosada, 26 November 2020

stops.name: Jardín Bella Vista, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: About thirty people bury him at the Jardín Bella Vista cemetery in San Miguel, beside his mother and his father, at the end of the same day the country has spent in the street. Two plaques go onto the grave: thanks to the ball, and we miss you. In March 2026, with Javier Milei in the Casa Rosada, the retrial of his doctors and nurses opens in San Isidro, and the last public record of him is a courtroom arguing about twelve hours in Benavídez. The trial is still running as this is compiled.

stops.name: Naples, the stadium takes his name
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nine days after the death the Naples city council votes unanimously to rename the San Paolo after him. It is the municipal stadium of a city of a million people and it now carries an Argentine's name. In the Quartieri Spagnoli, a mural Mario Filardi painted in 1990 has been repainted twice and stands over a square of offerings; in the Bar Nilo a lock of his hair sits in a glass urn among the images of San Gennaro and the Virgin of Pompeii. Naples had patron saints before he came.
suggested_refs: The renaming plaque at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona; the Largo Maradona mural, Via Emanuele De Deo 60
